messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At 62, Robert was a soft-spoken North American man who had spent most of his adult life at a potter’s wheel, shaping bowls and mugs in a small studio attached to the side of the house he shared with his wife. The death of his younger brother, Daniel, had changed the feel of that house in an instant. Daniel had died unexpectedly after a sudden cardiac event while the two men were setting up a community art fair together, still laughing over whether the glaze on Robert’s blue cups had come out too dark. Robert had seen him only minutes before the collapse, had stood there when the ambulance crew took over, and later had to answer the questions that came when it became clear that Daniel would not be coming back. What stayed with Robert was not only the shock of the scene but the abruptness of it: one minute Daniel was alive beside him, the next he was a memory everyone else seemed to handle better than Robert could.

In the months that followed, Robert found that anything that carried Daniel’s presence could catch him off guard. A particular cedar-smoke scent from the kiln area, the sound of men laughing at the hardware store, a song Daniel used to hum, even the sight of the folding tables he used for fairs could bring a hard stop to his day. He would turn away from family photographs and leave rooms when someone mentioned a holiday plan that Daniel should have been part of. At home, he began clearing away small reminders more quickly than anyone else noticed: Daniel’s old coffee mug, a flyer from the last exhibition they had discussed, a voicemail he could not bring himself to replay. He told himself it was easier not to open the door to that pain than to keep getting hit by it.

Robert also became wary of anything that made the loss feel present in a more hopeful way. When his wife suggested a weekend trip or mentioned booking a winter show, he felt a jolt of alarm rather than comfort. Positive feelings themselves had started to feel unsafe to him, as if enjoying a good day was an invitation for something terrible to be taken away again. If a kiln load came out especially well, or a customer praised his work, he noticed himself flattening his reaction, pushing the pleasure down before it could settle. He had come to believe that if he let himself feel too happy, he would be blindsided by another loss, and that belief made even ordinary moments of satisfaction feel fragile and suspect.

This had begun to narrow his world. Robert and his wife had once talked casually about taking a trip to visit their daughter in Oregon, but he now avoided making any future plans beyond the next few days. He would not commit to family gatherings, would not schedule fairs far in advance, and often put off decisions about the studio that used to come easily. The calendar on the kitchen wall stayed half empty. He said he did not want to promise anything he might not be able to bear, but beneath that was a deeper fear that looking ahead meant risking hope, and hope made room for disappointment. The result was that days became smaller and more repetitive, organized around what could be managed without imagining what might come next.

At work, this pattern followed him into the studio. Pottery had once been a place where Robert felt grounded, but now even there reminders waited: the empty stool Daniel used to sit on, the shelves where collaborative pieces had been stored, the possibility that a customer might ask about the man who had helped run the fair with him. He kept busy with trimming and glazing, yet part of him was always bracing for a wave of grief to break through. The less he allowed himself to feel, the more contained life became, until his wife noticed how often he seemed absent even when he was home. He had not been sleeping well and had grown quieter at meals, but what brought him to seek help was the sense that the narrowness was spreading. He was tired of having his days organized around what he could not bear to remember, and he was frightened by how strongly he still believed that joy, plans, and even ordinary hope might put him in harm’s way. What he wanted most was to be able to think of Daniel without immediately shutting down, and to live in a way that did not feel as though the future itself had become something to avoid.
